title: In Banning AI, Is Berkeley Law Shortchanging Its Students -- and Endangering their Future Clients?
author: Bob Ambrogi

dom.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption

st.t: AI curriculum: Assistance must preserve intellectual development
st.an: The source accepts the need for unaided foundational work while materially developing the cluster’s balanced approach: it argues that students should also practise supervising and verifying AI in low-stakes educational settings so they acquire context-specific professional judgment before client work.
qs: A first-year law student who never learns to read and analyze a case unaided by AI is poorly trained for the remainder of law school, let alone legal practice.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: Ambrogi accepts the cluster’s central aim of developing independent legal judgment alongside AI competence, while materially advancing it through a concrete integrated-assessment model: students critique and correct flawed AI work. He supports targeted foundational safeguards but argues that degree-wide restrictions impede supervised practice in verification and may defer errors to client work; that harm remains prospective rather than measured.
qs: An assignment that asks a student to critique and correct a deliberately flawed AI-generated brief simultaneously tests judgment and builds AI competency.

st.t: Law-school policy: Staged use bridges bans and adoption

He rejects Berkeley’s three-year restrictive default as overbroad, but does not advocate unrestricted assistance; his predicted client harms remain prospective.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Ambrogi accepts the cluster’s competence-risk premise—students need unaided foundational analysis—and materially extends its proposed response. He argues that verification and AI supervision are themselves competencies best developed through controlled, low-stakes classroom practice, offering a concrete assignment that combines independent legal judgment with error detection rather than choosing either blanket prohibition or unrestricted use.
qs: The only way to build that “judgment muscle” is to use it, and the best and safest place to use it is in law school, before AI mistakes can harm actual clients.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s supervised-AI model and extends it into legal education: students should first develop independent legal reasoning, particularly in the first year, while also learning to verify and supervise AI output rather than deferring AI competence entirely.
qs: A first-year law student who never learns to read and analyze a case unaided by AI is poorly trained for the remainder of law school, let alone legal practice.

That is not just the ability to use AI, but also to supervise it – to spot the hallucinated citation, to recognize when an AI outline has buried the strongest argument, to feel where a generated draft is confidently wrong.

kp.k: Berkeley sharply restricts AI in assessed legal education
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that Berkeley Law's policy, taking effect in summer 2026, prohibits generative AI across nearly every stage of producing graded work and outright in exams. It also prohibits uploading course materials into generative AI systems and restricts research use to identifying sources, which students must verify. These are reported institutional rules, not findings about their educational effects.
qs: The rule, which [the school released last week](https://www.law.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/AI-Final-Policy-26.pdf), forbids the use of AI for “conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.”
Students remain responsible for verifying those sources, and the policy warns that citations to nonexistent authorities “will raise a presumption of prohibited AI use.”

kp.k: Restrictions aim to preserve independent analytical judgment
kp.d: Policy coauthor Chris Hoofnagle argues that legal education must develop students' own reasoning rather than assess AI-assisted output quality. He says advances enabling models to produce whole research papers made Berkeley's 2023 policy too permissive. The article reports that, according to the San Francisco Chronicle, an uptick in submissions with dubious reasoning prompted the proposal; it supplies no quantitative evidence of that trend.
qs: “We want students to develop their own analytical judgment, otherwise they just outsource it to AI,” he wrote.
“Here’s a key idea: In the classroom, we don’t want students to write the best possible paper, but rather the best possible paper that the student is capable of.”
A model, he said, “can, in effect, write a research paper soup to nuts,” and that capability “required us to rethink students’ reliance on them.”

kp.k: Policy permits self-tutoring and instructor-authorized departures
kp.d: Despite Ambrogi's characterization of the policy as a blanket ban across all three years, the document reports important qualifications: students may use AI for class preparation and self-tutoring, instructors may authorize departures with written notice and disclosure requirements, and Berkeley offers AI-specific courses. Hoofnagle distinguishes these opportunities from foundational learning, particularly in the first year.
qs: Hoofnagle said that students remain free to use AI “to prepare for class, to self-tutor, and so on.”
“Instructors have the discretion to deviate from this default rule, provided that they do so in writing and with appropriate notice and require students to disclose any authorized AI use,” it states.
“But when it comes to the basics, particularly in 1L, we need students to do the work, lest they never develop the ability to judge for themselves.”

kp.k: Law firms reportedly expect AI-proficient graduates
kp.d: Ambrogi reports Hoofnagle's acknowledgment that firms expect graduates to possess AI skills and that students request training after encountering extensive AI use during summer internships. This is an attributed account of employer expectations and student demand, not a measured survey of adoption or hiring requirements.
qs: He told Business Insider that the expectation from law firms is that students graduate AI-proficient, and that students are themselves requesting these courses after learning during their summer internships that firms already use AI extensively.

kp.k: AI competency requires supervision, not merely tool operation
kp.d: Ambrogi argues that professional AI competence consists partly of human verification and substantive judgment: detecting fabricated citations, recognizing poorly prioritized arguments, and identifying confidently incorrect drafts. He contends that these capabilities require practice with AI rather than simply learning to operate it.
qs: That is not just the ability to use AI, but also to supervise it – to spot the hallucinated citation, to recognize when an AI outline has buried the strongest argument, to feel where a generated draft is confidently wrong.
The only way to build that “judgment muscle” is to use it, and the best and safest place to use it is in law school, before AI mistakes can harm actual clients.

kp.k: Broad restrictions may defer learning risks onto clients
kp.d: Ambrogi predicts that restricting classroom AI practice may postpone development of critical skills until summer associate placements or first-year practice, possibly without supervision. His proposed mechanism is displacement of mistakes from low-stakes educational settings into actual client matters; the document does not establish that the policy has caused client harm.
qs: The danger is that students do not develop critical AI skills until later, and then possibly without supervision, such as in a summer associate role or as a first-year lawyer, where the AI output they fail to scrutinize is attached to an actual client matter and the cost of a missed hallucination is no longer simply a grade.
A policy that removes AI from the one setting built for formative mistakes does not eliminate the possibility of mistakes – it simply defers them to the setting where they become more costly.

kp.k: Integrate foundational reasoning with supervised AI critique
kp.d: Ambrogi accepts that excessive AI reliance can prevent students from learning essential unaided legal analysis, but considers restrictions extending across all three years overbroad. He recommends combining analytical training with AI competency, exemplified by assignments requiring students to critique and correct deliberately flawed AI-generated briefs. This is a pedagogical proposal, not an evaluated intervention.
qs: There is a real risk that overuse of AI could cause students to effectively skip the foundational essentials of a legal education.
But in creating a blanket ban across all three years of law school, the rule seems misguidedly overbroad.
An assignment that asks a student to critique and correct a deliberately flawed AI-generated brief simultaneously tests judgment and builds AI competency.

kp.k: Embedded AI complicates enforcement and assessment design
kp.d: Hoofnagle acknowledges loopholes and enforcement difficulties because ordinary legal research and web-search tools increasingly incorporate AI. The article also reports Berkeley's conversion of some take-home exams to proctored, in-person assessments using lockdown software. Ambrogi predicts that Berkeley's standing may encourage other schools to study or copy its policy, without presenting evidence that such diffusion has occurred.
qs: Hoofnagle concedes the rule has loopholes and describes policing AI as a “Sisyphean task.”
He notes that standard searches on Lexis and Westlaw now surface LLM-generated summaries, and that search engines are layering AI over ordinary results.
“There is no kind of clean answer for it,” he told Business Insider, conceding the school “obviously can’t ban search.”
And given Berkeley’s standing and its history as an early mover on legal-tech education, still other schools will likely read this rule closely, and perhaps even copy it.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source presents competing claims about AI-era legal competence: reliance on AI can undermine foundational analytical judgment, while restricting supervised AI practice can leave graduates unprepared to verify its work and expose future clients to mistakes.
pts.d: Chris Hoofnagle argues that increasingly capable generative models enable students to outsource analysis and paper production, making restrictions necessary to preserve independent judgment, particularly in first-year education. Bob Ambrogi acknowledges that risk but argues that AI competence also requires practiced human supervision: detecting fabricated citations, identifying weak argument structures and recognizing incorrect drafts. Ambrogi predicts that broadly excluding AI from graded work may defer that learning to client-facing employment, where mistakes are more consequential. He proposes integrating analytical and AI skills through assignments that require students to critique and correct flawed AI output. Hoofnagle also reports that firms already expect AI-proficient graduates and use AI extensively. Both the reported presence of AI in ordinary research tools and Hoofnagle's comments indicate that enforcing a clean separation from AI is difficult. Ambrogi further predicts that other schools may copy Berkeley's policy.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on policy text, Hoofnagle's reported observations and statements, and Ambrogi's pedagogical reasoning—not quantitative evidence of learning outcomes or client harm.
pts.d: Ambrogi quotes Berkeley's policy to establish the restricted activities and its cognitive-skills rationale. Hoofnagle's case draws on observations of student work: Ambrogi reports, citing the San Francisco Chronicle, an uptick in submissions with dubious reasoning, and quotes Hoofnagle describing students who believed conversations with ChatGPT had produced original solutions already present in the literature. The claim about employer demand rests on Hoofnagle's statements to Business Insider, including reports of students discovering extensive firm AI use during internships. The enforcement claim is illustrated by AI summaries appearing in Lexis, Westlaw and search engines. Ambrogi's prediction of deferred mistakes and greater client risk is an argument about where learning occurs; the article supplies no measured comparison of educational policies, model benchmark, or documented client injury caused by this policy.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article describes current employer expectations and a policy taking effect in summer 2026; predicted harms arise later if students reach practice without sufficient supervised AI experience.
pts.d: The policy is described as taking effect 'this summer' in a source dated 2026. Hoofnagle ties its introduction to model advances since the school's 2023 policy. Ambrogi's risk prediction concerns subsequent summer associate placements and first-year legal practice, with no quantified horizon or probability. His objection is to restrictions across all three years, rather than foundational restrictions confined to first-year students. Important qualifications are that Berkeley offers AI-specific courses, allows preparation and self-tutoring uses, permits narrow source-identification research subject to verification, and gives instructors discretion to authorize departures in writing with disclosure. These exceptions qualify Ambrogi's characterization of a blanket ban and mean the text does not establish that all supervised AI learning is eliminated. His broader conclusion is explicitly conditional on AI supervision becoming an essential legal competence.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are law students, educators, law firms hiring graduates, and future clients whose matters may become the setting for inexperienced AI use.
pts.d: For students, Hoofnagle emphasizes developing independent analysis, while Ambrogi emphasizes gaining complementary competence in checking and supervising AI output before practice. Instructors must protect foundational learning while deciding whether and how to authorize AI-assisted assignments. Firms are described as already demanding AI proficiency from recruits, without distinguishing firm size or market segment. Summer associates and first-year lawyers are identified as roles in which postponed learning could occur with insufficient supervision. Future clients face the predicted consequences of missed AI errors in real matters. Other law schools may be affected through adoption of similar restrictions. The article does not make specific claims about staffing reductions, pricing, ALSP competition, or access to justice.
